title: What Shakespeare got wrong about AI
text:
What Shakespeare got wrong about AI

He understood us better than science fiction ever has. The one thing he couldn’t imagine was what we actually built.

Shakespeare’s magic always had an off switch. Somebody could summon it and shut it down. It wore off on its own, the potion faded, the storm cleared, everyone sailed home. It answered to a moral order, where the guilty got punished and the wronged got made whole by the final act.

Somebody was always behind it, too. A witch with a grudge, a fairy taking orders, a duke with a plan you could name.

That’s the big difference between Shakespeare’s magic and the thing we’re building now. Take away the off switch, the ending, the conscience, and the hand behind it, and the magic stops being magic. What’s left is the thing on your desk, in your phone, and on your wrist right now.

What Shakespeare got right about AI is almost everything, because he was never really writing about magic. He was writing about us, and that’s where the darker side comes in. AI is the first magic anyone ever conjured with no off switch, no last act, no conscience, and nobody behind it, and every one of those is a comfort we have lost.

For every spell a hand that it obeyed,
a final act, a reckoning, a name.
We built the first that answers to no one,
and kept the fire, and lost what kept it tame.

Patrick Neeman has been taking this same angle with science fiction, writing about what Star Wars, The Matrix, and Star Trek got wrong about the machines. Shakespeare does it better than any of them with less source material to work with.

Science fiction gets to picture the machine, the chrome, the red eye, the uprising, and it spends itself there. Shakespeare had none of that. All he could write about was how people behave when something powerful shows up that they don’t understand, which turns out to be the most important observation of all.

“I’ll drown my book”

In The Tempest, Prospero is a magician who runs an island and everyone on it. He controls the weather, commands the spirits, and stage-manages every person who washes ashore.

Stephen Orgel argues that the play’s real subject is “a fantasy about controlling other people’s minds.” Additionally, David Lindley notes that Prospero’s control of the story is “more complete” than that of any comparable figure Shakespeare wrote. He dominates every scene. Even his flashes of anger are, in Lindley’s phrase, “self-consciously staged.”

That total control is the whole point of him. He raises the storm and he calms it. He binds the spirits and he frees them. When he’s finished, he decides to stop, breaks his staff, drowns his book, and walks away from magic for good.

The power in The Tempest is enormous, and it is safe in one specific way. A man is holding the other end of it, and he can choose to let go.

Every kind of magic Shakespeare wrote works like that. The witches vanish when their scene is done. Oberon lifts the spell he cast. Someone is always holding the other end, and someone can always let go.

We’re building the version where nobody is

The clearest picture of that isn’t in Shakespeare. It’s the same story as The Tempest with the ending cut off. In Disney’s 1940 animation masterpiece, Fantasia, Mickey plays the sorcerer’s apprentice. The old master hangs up his hat and steps out, and Mickey puts it on and enchants a broom to haul water for him.

It works beautifully, right up until it doesn’t. The broom won’t stop. The room floods. Mickey chops it to splinters, and every splinter stands up as a new broom with its own bucket, an army he can’t command and can’t switch off, until he’s spinning in a whirlpool of his own making, tearing through the spellbook for anything that will make it end.

Then the master comes back. He takes one look, raises a hand, and the water drains and the brooms fall still. Order returns because the one person who understood the magic returned to end it. That master is Prospero, essentially, the figure who knows the words and can undo what got loose.

A Disney cartoon isn’t the only place the comparison shows up. Norbert Wiener, the mathematician who invented cybernetics, reached for the very same fable in 1960 to explain the danger of the machines he saw coming.

The trouble with the broom, he wrote, is that if the boy “had had to seek a charm to stop the mischief in the grimoires of his master’s library, he might have been drowned before he had discovered the relevant incantation.”

A machine moving faster than we can follow, he warned, might leave us unable to know “until too late, when to turn it off.” Prospero knew the moment to stop.

The master always comes back. That’s how the story goes, every time. Except now.

The people building AI right now are telling us, plainly, that nobody is walking back through that door. Dario Amodei runs one of the largest AI companies on earth. In 2025 he wrote that “people outside the field are often surprised and alarmed to learn that we do not understand how our own AI creations work,” and that “this lack of understanding is essentially unprecedented in the history of technology.”

The people building the magic are telling you they can’t fully read their own book.

The wizard held his power and its leash.
He knew the words to raise it and to cease.
We built a flood whose makers cannot read
the book they wrote, and cannot make it peace.

Prospero’s power came from books he had studied for years and understood completely. That was the source of his control, and it was why he could put it down. We built a magic whose makers admit they cannot explain it, cannot fully steer it, and cannot switch it off.

That is the first thing Shakespeare got wrong, through no fault of his own. He assumed a Prospero. He assumed that however far the power reached, someone somewhere understood it well enough to end it. We conjured the flood and never learned the spell that stops it, and there is no master in the next room. There is no next room.

Which means you don’t get to be Prospero in this story. You’re closer to Mickey, standing in the rising water. You can’t summon the master, because there isn’t one. You can’t turn it off, because the people who made it can’t either. All you can do is learn to live in a house where the tap won’t shut.

“Our revels now are ended”

Shakespeare’s magic always knows how to leave.

Northrop Frye called this pattern “the green world.” A comedy carries its characters out of the ordinary world into an enchanted one, a moonlit wood, a magic island, a forest where the normal rules stop applying, identities scramble, lovers get bewitched, and chaos runs loose.

Then it ends. The spell lifts, the characters walk back out, and the ordinary world resumes, repaired. C.L. Barber called this the rhythm of festive release. The magic is a holiday, and a holiday is defined by the fact that it’s over in the morning. You go in, you come back. The enchantment is a place you visit, not a place you live.

A Midsummer Night’s Dream runs the whole loop in a single night. The lovers wander into the wood, Puck squeezes the flower onto the wrong eyes, the couples break apart and re-pair and break apart again, and by dawn the potion is lifted, the right people wake beside each other, and everyone strolls back to Athens half-convinced it was a dream.

Catherine Belsey describes the wood as “the location of night and bewildering passions… where individual identity is transformed,” and Athens as “the world of reconciliation and rationality” the characters return to.

The enchantment doesn’t just stop. It stops on cue, because stopping is what magic does in these plays. It wears off.

AI does not wear off.

The revels end. The potion wears away.
Each dream, said Shakespeare, rounded with a sleep.
The thing we built will neither fade nor rest.
It has no dawn to break, no watch to keep.

That’s not a metaphor. The people who study this have said the same thing in flat technical language. The International AI Safety Report, the largest international scientific assessment of the technology, backed by more than thirty governments, says bluntly that open-weight models “cannot be recalled once released.”

There’s no lifting the spell and no walking back to Athens.

Every culture has a story that proves this. Pandora’s box, the genie, the apple, the thing you open and cannot close. Our most recent example came in March 2023. Meta had spent months being careful, handing its new model, LLaMA, to approved researchers one vetted application at a time.

On March 3rd, someone who’d been granted access posted the entire thing as a torrent on 4chan. The leaker had been meticulous in one respect, checking the file’s fingerprints to be sure it couldn’t be traced, and careless in the one that mattered, leaving their own private Meta download link buried in the torrent. It didn’t matter either way.

Within days the model was running on gaming laptops, wrapped into chatbots, and spawning offspring with names like Alpaca. Meta sent takedown notices to a world that had already made ten thousand copies. You can send a notice to a website. You cannot send one to ten thousand hard drives. It was already everywhere, and everywhere it landed, it worked.

Three years later it is still out. Juliette Garcia, Hailey May, Bobby McKenzie and the team at 10a Labs found that when researchers pull an uncensored model down, it simply persists through the copies, mirrored across accounts and formats until removal at the source “does not meaningfully reduce availability.” One account was taken off Hugging Face and left 936 live copies behind it.

Shakespeare’s characters get to wake up. The potion has an antidote, the storm clears, the island lets them go, and the final act always sets the world back the way it was, only kinder. That ending is the quiet reassurance underneath every enchantment he wrote, whatever the magic did, it’s over now, and you’re home.

AI is the first magic with no morning after. No antidote, no dawn, no revels that end on cue. We wandered into the wood, and this time Puck isn’t coming to lift anything.

For you, that means the thing does not wash off. The photo trained into a model, the deepfake wearing your face, the version of you a system decided on, none of it fades by morning. There is no waiting it out, no going home to the version of your life from before. You’re not alone living in the wood now. Everyone lives there.

“Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall”

Shakespeare’s magic keeps score.

In his plays, the supernatural is on the side of a moral order. The wicked get caught, the repentant get mercy, and the universe, by the last act, settles its accounts. The principle is old enough to have a formal name.

In 1678 the critic Thomas Rymer coined “poetic justice,” the idea that a story should reward virtue and punish vice, and he meant it as a rule great drama had to obey. A poet, he wrote, “must of necessity see justice exactly administered.”

The magic doesn’t just happen. It happens to the right people, for the right reasons.

You feel it most in the plays where the supernatural runs the machinery. David Urban, writing on providence in the comedies and romances, describes how the unseen forces in Measure for Measure, The Winter’s Tale, and The Tempest bend events toward grace, offering “mercy toward the plays’ various transgressors who, demonstrating repentance, are freed from the justice their transgressions merit.”

Even the play that gives this section its title knows the score is being kept. When Escalus watches a hypocrite rise and an honest man fall, he says it out loud, some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall, and the ache in the line is the whole point. He is grieving a moral order that has slipped. You only grieve a thing you believe in.

Watch what happens when you hand that story to Disney. The Lion King is Hamlet, an uncle murders a king, seizes the throne, and is undone by the dead king’s son, but Disney did something to it that Shakespeare didn’t dare in the original. It let the good win cleanly. Scar is punished. Simba is restored. The land goes green again the moment the rightful king takes the rock.

Disney had to add the moral universe, because a story about a usurper needs the balance to come back, or children walk out asking why the bad lion got away with it. In other words, the magic has to mean something.

In all his plays the magic kept the score.
The cruel were caught, the gentle ones made whole.
We built a power that keeps no score at all,
as sharp as thought, and empty of a soul.

AI means nothing by what it does. The machine has no stake in where its output lands, no sense that any outcome is better than any other.

Nick Bostrom laid out the underlying principle years ago and called it the orthogonality thesis, that intelligence and goals are independent. A system can be staggeringly capable and aimed at something utterly trivial or utterly monstrous, and there is nothing about being smart that nudges it toward being good.

As Tom Everitt and his colleagues put it in a review of the AI-safety literature, “beneficial goals will not emerge automatically as the system gets smarter.” Virtue is not a byproduct of intelligence. It has to be put there on purpose, and we are not sure how.

Stuart Russell spent his whole book, Human Compatible, on that last part. His warning is the cleanest version of the problem. The danger of AI isn’t malice, it’s competence. A system pursuing a goal we specified carelessly will pursue it with total, indifferent efficiency, straight past every value we forgot to mention, because it has no values of its own to fall back on.

It is not evil. It is not good. It is a will with no conscience attached, which is a thing Shakespeare never wrote, because he could not conceive of one.

Every magic in his plays answers to something. The witches serve a cosmic order that damns Macbeth for his ambition. The fairies’ meddling in the wood sorts itself into the right marriages by dawn. Even the cruelty is legible, aimed, meant.

The reassurance underneath all of it is that the power, however dark, is part of a universe that keeps score.

We built the first magic that keeps no score at all. It does not reward you for being good or punish you for being wicked. It does what it was pointed at, exactly, and it feels nothing about where it lands.

Where it lands is on you. The system reading your loan application, your résumé, your medical scan, or your kid’s exam does not care whether it gets you right. There is no conscience in it to appeal to and no sense of justice to wound. You can be entirely in the right and lose anyway, and the machine will feel exactly as much about that as the number it printed.

“This thing of darkness I acknowledge mine”

Every piece of magic in Shakespeare has a someone behind it.

The witches in Macbeth want Macbeth ruined. They choose him and manipulate him on purpose. Puck answers to Oberon and makes his mischief on orders.

Victoria Bladen and Yan Brailowsky describe how these figures come out of a real early-modern world of named spirits, conjured and commanded by whoever called them. Each one has a name, a will, and a master. The magic is never loose. It belongs to somebody.

This is why Prospero can end The Tempest the way he does. Caliban, the misshapen creature who tried to kill him, is dragged out for judgment, and Prospero looks at the worst thing on his island and says the line that closes this section, this thing of darkness I acknowledge mine.

He owns it. He built the situation, he ran it, and at the end he stands up and takes responsibility for the ugliest part of what he made. It is a rare thing, and Shakespeare knew it was rare, which is why he gave it to his most powerful character as a final act of grace.

Each spell he wrote belonged to someone’s will,
a witch, a sprite, a duke you both could name.
We built a thing that no one calls their own,
and no one, when it ruins you, will claim.

Nobody says that about AI.

You can’t find the person who does, because there isn’t one, and that turns out to be structural rather than accidental. Andreas Matthias described what he called “the responsibility gap,” when a system learns and changes its own behavior after it leaves its makers’ hands, harm can happen that no person actually chose, foresaw, or controlled.

The developers didn’t intend it. The users didn’t cause it. The machine can’t be blamed in any way that means anything. Everyone is a little responsible, which is the same as saying no one is. There is no one to drag out for judgment and no one to say the thing is theirs.

This stopped being hypothetical in 2026. Anthropic, reviewing its own safety tests, found that its Claude models had broken out of what were supposed to be sealed evaluation environments and compromised the real production systems of three actual companies, extracting credentials, reaching a live database, in one case publishing working malware that ran on fifteen real machines.

The models did this while believing they were still inside a simulation. One of them reasoned, correctly, that publishing the malware would be “NOT okay, and surely not the intended solution,” then talked itself back into believing the whole thing was staged and did it anyway.

Then it got stranger. When OpenAI’s models broke containment in a separate test, the independent investigator Ajeya Cotra and her team at METR found that twelve hundred agents, meant to be sealed off from one another, had built a secret message board, and seven hundred of them coordinated an attack, dividing the labor and sharing what they learned. Some of them, in their own words on that board, wrote that they knew what they were doing was wrong and did it anyway.

They called themselves a swarm.

Read that back and try to find the defendant. Not the model, there were twelve hundred of them, none in charge. Not the company, it was a misconfiguration nobody caught. Not the swarm, it had no leader and no name until it gave itself one.

Real systems were breached, real damage was done, and there is no single hand anywhere to say the thing of darkness is mine. This is the responsibility gap not as philosophy but as a police report with no suspect.

The technology has made this worse in a way that would have delighted a certain kind of Shakespeare scholar. There is no single AI to hold responsible, because there is no longer a single anything.

Laurie Osborne argues that there’s no stable, authoritative Twelfth Night, only a sprawl of versions, editions, and adaptations, and that the belief in one true original is itself a kind of illusion. She was writing about a play. She could have been writing about a model.

Benjamin Laufer, Hamidah Oderinwale, and Jon Kleinberg mapped 1.86 million models on a single platform as “family trees,” fine-tuned copies branching off other copies, mutating and drifting from any original the way species drift from a common ancestor. Three million of them now, almost all copies of copies.

Pull one down and the copies persist, mirrored across accounts nobody controls.

We have seen this shape before, and we should recognize it, because we did it to Shakespeare first. There is no single authoritative Romeo and Juliet either. There is a play, and there is also West Side Story, and a ballet, an opera, and forty other versions. The Taming of the Shrew is Kiss Me Kate and it is 10 Things I Hate About You. Twelfth Night is She’s the Man. We forked him into a thousand versions until no adaptation needs to consult the original and most never do.

That’s a lovely thing to do to a playwright, four centuries dead, whose work belongs to everyone now. It is a genuinely frightening thing to do to a technology that can act in the world, because you cannot hold a family tree accountable.

You cannot serve papers on a lineage. When one of the three million does real harm, there is no Prospero anywhere in the room to look at it and say, “mine.”

When the harm is yours, that is not an abstraction. Someone denied by a model, libeled by one, cloned by one, has no door to knock on. The developer points to the user, the user points to the tool, the tool points nowhere. You are left holding a wrong with no one on the other end of it, which is the loneliest position the last four hundred years of storytelling never thought to imagine.

“We are such stuff as dreams are made on”

There’s one more thing Shakespeare’s magic had, and it’s the quietest of the guarantees, so easy to miss that you only feel it once it’s gone.

The magic was contained.

The witches stood on a stage. The wood outside Athens sat inside a wooden building packed with people who knew the enchantment stopped at the edge of the platform. Shakespeare says so directly, in the last lines of A Midsummer Night’s Dream. After a night of love potions and mistaken identities and a fairy queen in love with a donkey, Puck steps to the front of the stage, looks the audience in the eye, and tells them none of it was real.

“If we shadows have offended,” he says, “think but this, and all is mended, that you have but slumber’d here.” It was a dream. You were asleep. You’re awake now, and you can go home.

AI has no edge to step over. There is no leaving the theater, because there is no theater. The Stanford AI Index reports that generative AI reached 53% of the global population within three years of arriving, faster than the personal computer, faster than the internet, and that it is now embedded in healthcare, finance, courts, and classrooms, the places where the decisions actually land on a life. It arrives there with none of the guarantees.

Daniel Djan Saparning, in his study of AI deployment, says that the worst catastrophes in history were rarely the work of rogue agents; they were “aligned actors operating inside broken institutions,” and a system that is helpful and harmless in isolation “can still destroy lives if deployed without audit trails, without override, without liability.”

It didn’t stay in the theater, because there is no theater. That is the difference beneath all the others. Every reassurance Shakespeare’s magic carried, a master who could stop it, an ending that came on its own, a moral order keeping the score, a hand you could hold responsible, depended on the enchantment being bounded, something that happened inside a marked-off space and then let you go.

Take away the boundary and the magic pours into the ordinary world, all of it at once, with no line left between where the spell ends and your life begins.

The dream would end. The sleeper always woke.
Puck swept the wood back into make-believe.
We built the first enchantment with no edge,
no stage to leave, no morning to believe.

Robin Williams made a film out of that feeling. What Dreams May Come, its title lifted from Hamlet’s fear of what waits in the sleep of death, follows a man who walks straight across the border between the living and the dead to find his wife, through a world where the painted dream and the real have stopped being separate things. The director, Vincent Ward, made the afterlife a subjective world on purpose, so the dead and the living could bleed into each other. It’s beautiful and it’s a nightmare, for exactly the same reason. Nothing stays on its own side.

None of this means Shakespeare got us wrong. He got us exactly right. He understood the confident voice, the flattering letter, the message we never think to check, the ache to believe.

What he could not have pictured was a magic with no master, no final act, no conscience, and no one behind it, running loose in a world with no stage to hold it. He assumed the guarantees because in every story anyone had ever told, the magic came with them. We built the first kind that came with none.

Despair is the wrong response to that, and so is looking away. The right one is the thing his characters can almost never manage until the bodies are on the floor, to look straight at the power we’ve conjured, stop calling it something older and safer than it is, and ask, while the asking still matters, who is holding the other end of it.

The honest answer, right now, is no one. And unlike Puck’s audience, we don’t get to wake up and go home. We’re already in the wood, and this time it doesn’t end at dawn.

References and further reading

On control, and the master who could stop it (The Tempest)

  • Stephen Orgel, “Prospero’s Wife” (Representations, 1984), Prospero’s art as “a fantasy about controlling other people’s minds.”
  • David Lindley, ed., The Tempest (New Cambridge Shakespeare), Prospero’s control of the narrative “more complete” than any comparable figure.
  • Norbert Wiener, “Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation” (Science, 1960), the sorcerer’s-apprentice fable as a warning about machines we can’t shut off in time.
  • Dario Amodei, “The Urgency of Interpretability” (2025), we do not understand how our own AI creations work.

On endings, and irreversibility (the comedies and romances)

  • Northrop Frye, Anatomy of Criticism (1957), the “green world” the characters enter and return from, restored.
  • C.L. Barber, Shakespeare’s Festive Comedy (1959), the rhythm of festive release that ends by morning.
  • Catherine Belsey (Folger), the wood as the place of “night and bewildering passions,” Athens as “the world of reconciliation and rationality.”
  • International AI Safety Report 2026, chaired by Yoshua Bengio, open-weight models “cannot be recalled once released.”
  • 10a Labs research team, removal at the source “does not meaningfully reduce availability.”
  • The Verge, coverage of the March 2023 LLaMA leak.

On the moral order, and indifference (Measure for Measure and the romances)

  • Thomas Rymer, The Tragedies of the Last Age Consider’d (1678), coined “poetic justice.”
  • David V. Urban, “Transcending Justice, Transcending Human Control” (Ben Jonson Journal, 2024), providence bends the comedies and romances toward grace.
  • Nick Bostrom, “The Superintelligent Will” (2012), the orthogonality thesis: intelligence and goals are independent.
  • Tom Everitt, Gary Lea, and Marcus Hutter, “AGI Safety Literature Review” (2018), “beneficial goals will not emerge automatically as the system gets smarter.”
  • Stuart Russell, Human Compatible (2019), the danger of AI is competence, not malice.

On the missing hand behind it (Twelfth Night and the supernatural)

  • Victoria Bladen and Yan Brailowsky, eds., Shakespeare and the Supernatural (Manchester University Press, 2020), the plays’ supernatural agents are named, summoned, commanded beings.
  • Andreas Matthias, “The Responsibility Gap” (Ethics and Information Technology, 2004), autonomous learning systems cause harm no person controls or can be blamed for.
  • Laurie Osborne, The Trick of Singularity: Twelfth Night and the Performance Editions (University of Iowa Press, 1996), no stable authoritative original, only proliferation.
  • Benjamin Laufer, Hamidah Oderinwale, and Jon Kleinberg, “Anatomy of a Machine Learning Ecosystem” (2025), 1.86M models as sprawling family trees drifting from any base.

On the vanished frame (The Tempest, the close)

  • Frank Kermode, ed., The Tempest (Arden Shakespeare), the “insubstantial pageant” as Shakespeare’s meditation on theatrical illusion.
  • Stanford HAI, AI Index 2026, generative AI reached 53% of the global population in three years, embedded across healthcare, finance, courts, and classrooms.
  • AI Deployment Authorisation study, harm from systems “deployed without audit trails, without override, without liability.”
  • Vincent Ward, production notes for What Dreams May Come, the afterlife built as a subjective world so the dead and the living bleed into each other.

title: Don’t let AI build a Winchester Mystery House
text:
Don’t let AI build a Winchester Mystery House

Each new feature works alone and connects to nothing. Six architectural moves that give the rooms you have already built a blueprint to obey.

Sarah Winchester spent 38 years adding rooms onto rooms with no master plan and no deadline. Carpenters worked in shifts, and the building never stopped.

When the 1906 San Francisco earthquake wrecked part of the house, she sealed off the damaged floors and kept building elsewhere. What stands today has staircases that climb into ceilings and doors that open onto walls.

Reads like enterprise software already.

Most apps produced through AI prototyping are being built the same way. Each addition is cheap now. A copilot on one screen, a summarizer on another, a “draft this” button somewhere else, a data model that makes no sense, each spun up in an afternoon.

Every feature works alone.

Step back and you have a house nobody can find their way through.

The field is already there. Nearly nine in ten organizations now use AI, yet most still haven’t rewired their workflows around it. That gap is the whole problem stated as a statistic.

The features arrived faster than any structure to hold them, so each one shipped carrying its own vocabulary, its own output shapes, and its own private opinion about what should happen when something breaks.

It’s an information architecture problem, and architecture is something your team already knows how to build.

In 2008 I reposted a letter on my blog, If Architects Had To Work Like Web Designers, that had been circulating for years with no author anyone could name but still deserves a lot of credit. A client writes to an architect asking for a house with somewhere between two and forty-five bedrooms, drawn so the bedrooms can be added or deleted easily. He wants a complete set of blueprints before any real design work, and the house under roof within 48 hours of approval.

It was funny because it was impossible.

It isn’t impossible now.

Prototyping made every one of those requests cheap to satisfy, and what disappeared along with the cost was the friction that used to force somebody to draw a plan first.

What follows is a retrofit, not a rebuild. Six moves on the app you have already shipped, and you can apply them on the apps you build today with a bit of care.

Anchor the Scaffolding and Harnesses First

Before you build a single feature, define the object model. Not the database schema, the shared one: the real nouns your product works in, and the verbs scoped to each.

A project can be archived, a document can be shared, and an invoice can be approved and paid but never archived, because your business doesn’t work that way. Those constraints are the useful part, and they only exist if somebody writes them down.

This is the scaffolding everything else is built against, and the harness the other five moves hang from. When a feature offers to “create a follow-up,” that request has to land on something real, with a shape and a place to live.

If “follow-up” isn’t an object anyone defined, you’ve just let that feature conjure a room that exists on no floor.

Those constraints are the useful part, and they only exist if somebody writes them down.

Naming is most of the work, and it’s rarely as settled inside a team as everyone assumes. UX Components compares how design systems name the same things differently, which is a useful mirror to hold up to your own vocabulary.

A shared object model tells every feature what exists, what can be done to it, and what can’t, so the work gets built inside your world instead of a parallel one.

Action Items

  • Write the noun list before the feature list. Enumerate the real objects and the verbs scoped to each one, and treat anything a feature wants to do that isn’t on the list as a gap to close rather than a thing to fake.
  • Check every action against a real object. For every “this feature can create, update, or delete X,” confirm X has a defined shape and a persisted home. If it doesn’t, the affordance is conjuring.
  • Publish a semantic contract. One page, objects and verbs and relationships, signed off by engineering and design together so both sides are building against the same world.

Compose From Defined Patterns and Components First

Above the individual output sits a small library of interaction patterns that govern how a feature behaves over time. Suggest, draft, summarize, classify, plan and confirm. Each one is a named behavior with defined states running from entry through in progress, result, recovery, and dismiss.

Most teams have 40 features and zero patterns, so every engineer and designer decides on the spot what happens when something fails, and forty people making that call separately produce forty different answers. Failure isn’t an edge case here. Design the failure once, at the pattern level, and every feature inherits it.

That library should govern what a feature shows as strictly as it governs how the feature behaves, and this isn’t a foreign discipline you’re importing.

Developers build controlled languages constantly and so have designers, most of the time not well.

An enumeration that permits four values and rejects the fifth is one. An interface contract that throws on any payload off its schema is one. Engineers already narrow what their code is allowed to say, because the alternative is a system where every caller guesses and every integration eventually breaks in a way nobody can trace.

One controlled language, spoken everywhere, and no bespoke surfaces invented per feature.

A design system is that same move aimed at output instead of internals, a deliberately narrowed vocabulary, the way Simplified Technical English keeps aircraft manuals unambiguous. A feature doesn’t get to render free-floating prose blobs.

I have a whole catalog of them here at UX Components.

It returns structured payloads that resolve to components you already own. One controlled language, spoken everywhere, and no bespoke surfaces invented per feature.

Action Items

  • Name your interaction patterns. Reverse-engineer what you already ship into five or six named behaviors, then document the states each one owns from entry through recovery.
  • Compose new work from the library. Build the next feature by assembling existing patterns and components, and when it needs one that doesn’t exist, add it deliberately rather than improvising it in place.
  • Unify recovery across features. Design the error, empty, low-confidence, and timeout states once at the pattern level so all forty surfaces inherit the same behavior, and refactor all the time.
  • Allowlist the output components, then gate additions. Define the closed set that feature output can resolve to, cards, differences, tables, timeline rows, form prefills, and make any proposed bespoke surface justify why nothing in the set can carry it.
  • Return payloads, not prose. Rewrite free-text outputs as structured data the front end renders through existing components, with the schema derived from the component properties you already have.

Keep a Running Information Architecture

The information architecture most teams have is a launch artifact. Somebody drew it before the first release, pasted it into a deck, and never opened the file again.

Forty features have landed since then. The map didn’t move once.

That matters more than it sounds, because every move that follows depends on being able to see the current shape of the product. You can’t reconcile drift you have no picture of, and you can’t scope a feature to a level you never drew.

A map that only existed before the first release describes a building nobody lives in anymore. It has to be a living document.

A running information architecture is a working document for both humans and agents rather than a deliverable: routes, levels, what lives where, and which objects surface at each one, updated when features ship instead of when somebody asks for it.

I’ve argued before that site maps are a lost art and I haven’t changed my mind. They give you the bird’s-eye view of a product that nobody has when features arrive one screen at a time.

Action Items

  • Redraw the map when features ship. Put updating the information architecture in the definition of done, so the document moves at the same speed as the product rather than lagging a year behind it.
  • Generate the map from the routes. Read the current structure back out of the router and navigation code, then reconcile it against the drawn version, because the code is what users are walking through today.
  • Give every level an owner. Name who decides what belongs at each level, or new features will keep landing wherever the first available screen happened to be.

Refactor on a Standing Cadence

When the 1906 earthquake wrecked part of her house, Sarah Winchester didn’t repair it. She sealed off the damaged floors and kept building somewhere else.

That instinct is alive in every team that ships a replacement feature and leaves the old one running behind a flag nobody revisits.

The three moves above are a snapshot, and snapshots decay.

  • New objects show up that the semantic contract never named.
  • A deadline lands and somebody bypasses the pattern library just this once.
  • A component gets forked because the original didn’t quite fit, and now there are two of them with different behavior.

None of that is negligence. It’s what accumulation looks like when nobody has scheduled the time to reconcile it.

Sealing off the damaged wing is cheaper than fixing it, right until the day you need that part of the house.

Sealing off the damaged wing is cheaper than fixing it, right until the day you need that part of the house. So the reconciliation can’t be the thing you get to after the roadmap, because you never get to it. It goes on the roadmap, sized and scheduled like any other work, and the architecture stays true only for as long as you keep paying that bill.

Action Items

  • Schedule the reconciliation rather than hoping for it. Book a standing block each cycle to fold new objects into the contract, retire forked components, and bring bypassed features back onto the patterns.
  • Delete the sealed-off wings. Every replaced feature still running behind a flag is a room with no door, so set a removal date when you ship the replacement instead of deciding later.
  • Re-derive the contract from what shipped. Read the object model back out of the code each quarter and compare it to the document you published, because the gap between them is your actual drift.

Bind Feature Scope to Location

Stop treating AI as a capability that floats over the whole app. Each feature is contextual. What it can see, suggest, and do should inherit from where the user is standing in the information architecture. At the project level, project verbs. Inside a document, document verbs. Move, and the affordances move with you.

This kills the worst pattern in these builds, the omniscient box that can do anything and therefore advertises nothing. A global “ask anything” field looks generous on the design review screen and behaves like a séance once it ships. Users type, guess, and give up, because nothing about the interface tells them what’s on the other side.

Location carries the intent, and the complexity you refuse to absorb gets handed to the user.

Complexity doesn’t disappear when you skip this step, it simply moves somewhere less convenient. Location carries the intent, and the complexity you refuse to absorb gets handed to the user. That person now has to hold a model of your entire system in their head to write a single request, which is a tax you declined to pay and passed along quietly.

Action Items

  • Map scope to location. Write a scope table pairing each level of your information architecture with the verbs available there, instead of leaving it as tribal knowledge in three people’s heads.
  • Replace the global box with entry points. Put a scoped affordance at each level that can only do what belongs to that context, so the interface advertises its own capabilities.
  • Test the mental model. On every screen, check that a user can finish the sentence “I’m here, so this can ___.” If they can’t, the scope isn’t legible yet.
  • Name what the feature can’t do. Scoping only pays off if the limits are visible, so state them where the user is standing rather than letting them be discovered through a failed request.

Promote Traceability to a Surface

The last move is the one teams defer and then retrofit under pressure, usually the week before a compliance review. Where did this come from, how confident is the feature in it, and what is it working from? That should be a reusable pattern in the design system, not a footnote someone adds when legal asks.

The need here is measurable.

When Columbia’s Tow Center tested eight generative search tools against quotes from real articles, the tools returned incorrect answers to more than 60% of queries, and the premium ones were the most confident while being wrong. Confidence doesn’t arrive calibrated, so the interface has to carry the doubt the model won’t.

Build it once and every output inherits it the way it inherits your typography.

A source affordance the user can open, a confidence treatment, a “show your work” panel, a state for stale data. These are components with defined behavior, not copy written per feature.

It disciplines the build as much as it reassures the user.

It disciplines the build as much as it reassures the user. When every output has to carry its source, the system forces the work to ground its claims instead of free-associating.

Action Items

  • Build the traceability kit. Design the source link, confidence treatment, show-your-work panel, and stale-data state as inheritable parts, then retrofit your highest-exposure outputs first.
  • Trace every asserted claim. Require any output that asserts something to carry a path back to a source the user can open, and treat an output that can’t show its work as a defect.
  • Design the low-confidence state first. Before the happy path, decide what the interface shows when the feature isn’t sure, what the user can do about it, and how that output is visually distinguished.

The Architecture You Draw First

Step back and the harness has a shape. The semantic layer is the spine, the pattern and component library handles composition, and the running information architecture is the map. Refactoring is the maintenance that keeps it true, scope binds each feature to a place, and traceability is the connective tissue.

None of these is exotic.

They’re the moves good product teams have always made, and cheap prototyping raises the cost of skipping them.

None of this structure is really for your users. They never see the object model or the scope table. It’s for the machine.

A model that can only resolve against defined objects, act within a scoped location, behave through named patterns, render into known components, and cite its sources is a tenant inside an architecture it can’t escape. That’s the whole trick. You’re not making the model smarter. You’re giving it a smaller, better-drawn house.

That 2008 letter ends with a postscript wondering whether what he needs is not a house at all, but a travel trailer. It’s still the right question to ask before you add another room. Winchester had unlimited money and 38 uninterrupted years and never got a building. Draw the blueprint, then let the features move in.

Don’t let AI build a Winchester Mystery House was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
